title: SAR Flood Detection & ML Susceptibility Mapping — Layyah District, Pakistan
description: An open, reproducible remote-sensing study coupling dual-polarisation Sentinel-1 SAR inundation detection, bi-temporal SAR change detection, and an event-based machine-learning flood susceptibility model across Layyah District, Punjab (6,354 km²). Built entirely on open data and released with full GIS exports, training data, and a documented model card.
highlights: Random Forest F1 = 0.962, IoU = 0.928, ROC-AUC = 0.996 on held-out flood events
Chronological event-based validation (train 2003–2014, test 2015–2018) to structurally prevent temporal leakage
19 documented flood events from the Global Flood Database; 547.8 km² (8.6% of district) mapped as high susceptibility
Documents a silent-failure mode in Google Earth Engine raster distance operators that depressed model IoU by 0.025

gallery.caption: Modelled flood susceptibility, Layyah District
Study area: Layyah District, Punjab
ROC and precision-recall on held-out events

title: Land-Cover and Carbon Projection to 2043 — Lahore District, Pakistan
description: Four classified Landsat epochs (1993, 2003, 2013, 2023) projected forward to 2033 and 2043 with a CA-Markov model: Markov transition matrices set how much of each conversion happens, a Random Forest transition potential sets where, and a competitive cellular-automata allocation places it. Back-validated against years that can actually be checked before any projection was produced.
highlights: Not deep learning, deliberately. Four time points cannot train a temporal network; an LSTM over four epochs would be fitting noise and calling it sophistication. CA-Markov with a Random Forest transition potential is the defensible method at this data density.

Validation comes before projection. Calibrating on 1993–2003 and predicting 2013 gives a Figure of Merit of 0.215; calibrating on 2003–2013 and predicting 2023 gives 0.266. A null model that predicts no change scores 0.000. The pipeline refuses to project if the model cannot beat that null.

Overall accuracy is reported alongside, and it sits below the null model (0.638 against 0.778 in the 2023 test) because the model over-predicts change. Quoting the Figure of Merit alone would be selective, so both are published.

An earlier carbon parameterisation assigned the vegetation class 150 Mg C/ha, a closed-forest value, to a district of irrigated rice-wheat cropland. Measured on the maps it overstated the 1993–2023 carbon loss 5.9-fold. Corrected to IPCC Tier 1 cropland densities, with a low/best/high band on every figure.

The Earth Engine exports carried no nodata value, so masked pixels were written as 0 — the built-up class code — putting 1.80 million pixels, 44% of each raster, into the city. Statistics printed inside GEE were unaffected; anything computed from the files in QGIS or InVEST was not. The district was recovered to within 2% of its published extent.

Bare land changes class in 58–82% of its pixels per decade, which is Landsat confusing dry soil with concrete rather than land change. A three-class sensitivity run merging it into built-up improves every validation metric, and both runs are published so the choice can be argued rather than assumed.

Taken to national scale as a live companion app — see "Pakistan Land Cover and Carbon, 1993–2023" below — cross-checking this district's findings against an independent land-cover product (GLC-FCS30D) across all of Pakistan.

gallery.caption: Observed 1993–2023 and projected 2033–2043. Built-up rises from 20% of the district to 45% over the observed period.
Built-up change 1993–2023: 49,760 ha new (28.7% of the district) against 7,874 ha apparently lost — that second figure is classification instability, not de-urbanisation.
Class areas, observed solid and projected dashed. Growth decelerates because the Markov chain saturates, not because expansion is expected to slow.
Carbon stock with its uncertainty band, plotted against the original forest-density parameterisation that overstated the loss 5.9-fold.
Carbon density, 2023. Legend is discrete because density is assigned per class rather than measured, so only four values occur.
Projected 2043. Two Markov steps beyond the last observation, reported with its uncertainty rather than as a crisp forecast.

title: Pakistan Land Cover and Carbon, 1993–2023 — National Interactive App
description: The Lahore-district study above, taken to national scale: a live Streamlit app accounting land-cover change and terrestrial carbon for all of Pakistan (864,256 km²) from GLC-FCS30D at 30 m, district by district, with every figure traceable to the pixels behind it. Built as a companion to the district-level CA-Markov work, using an independent land-cover product (GLC-FCS30D rather than classified Landsat) as a national-scale cross-check.
highlights: 58,554 km² of Pakistan (6.8%) changed land-cover class between 2000 and 2022; the other 93.2% persisted and is deliberately excluded from the change diagram, where it would otherwise be one band wide enough to hide every real transition

The net national carbon flux is reported as +52.52 Tg C, but its uncertainty band runs -470.8 to +580.3 Tg C — spans zero, so the app states plainly that the sign is not established rather than presenting the point estimate as a finding

Caught and quantified a seasonal-snow artefact: the permanent-ice class swings 14% in nine years nationally (16,105 → 19,875 → 16,912 km², 2000/2013/2022), which permanent ice cannot physically do. About 5% of gross carbon loss traces to this snow/no-snow classification noise, not land change, and the app reports the flux with and without it

Every number is reproducible from cached tables with no live Earth Engine session required, so the app functions even when Earth Engine access is unavailable — every figure is footnoted with the exact accounting scale and source

gallery.caption: National net carbon flux, 2000–2022: the uncertainty band spans zero, so the point estimate (+52.5 Tg C) is reported as a centre, not a finding.

title: Urban Flood Analysis — Islamabad & Rawalpindi, 2026
description: Sentinel-1 SAR, GPM precipitation and terrain analysis for the twin cities, prompted by the 1 September 2026 flooding that raised Leh Nullah to 29 ft at Kattarian. The headline result is a sampling measurement rather than a flood map: Sentinel-1 structurally cannot observe flooding that drains in hours. Ends in a flood-proneness map that is published as explicitly unvalidated.
highlights: 0 of 86 heavy-rain half-hours in July–August 2026 were observable by Sentinel-1 — a 12-day revisit at a fixed 18:12 PKT overpass cannot catch flooding that lasts hours; the closest any pass came to heavy rain was 14.7 hours
The best available 'after' image (22 Aug, 13:12 UTC) precedes its own storm by four hours: the rain began ≈17:00 UTC and peaked at 23 mm/hr near 21:30 UTC
Backscatter rose almost everywhere (+1.07 dB open, +1.19 dB built-up) — the wet-soil dielectric response after 152 mm of antecedent rain, not standing water; 9 pixels in 4,008 were flagged as flooded

Urban double-bounce is stated as documented physics and explicitly not claimed as a finding: measured brightening is flat at 64–69% across every built-up class, where double-bounce would rise with density

Flood-proneness index over HAND, imperviousness, wetness index, slope and upstream area puts 137 km² of the 348 km² built-up area at high risk, concentrated along Leh Nullah where evacuations were ordered
Published as unvalidated: both available checks carry 9 and 11 positives, which is not bad luck but the direct consequence of the sampling result above

Every storm against every Sentinel-1 overpass: none coincide
July–August 2026 rainfall; the 1 September event post-dates all satellite products

title: Thermal Soil Moisture with TOTRAM — Layyah District, Pakistan
description: A Landsat 8/9 thermal-optical trapezoid (TOTRAM) soil moisture retrieval over Layyah District, built across 302 scenes (2019–2024) — and a negative result. The thermal trapezoid recovers no rainfall signal here under any of five ways of fitting it, while the optical retrieval (OPTRAM) reaches r = +0.86 on the same district, same bare-soil definition and same reference. Published as an evaluation rather than a product, because the maps look entirely convincing and only the validation says otherwise.
highlights: Five trapezoid specifications tested rather than one — per-scene, gated, pooled, per-month, per-month gated — giving r = −0.012, −0.031, −0.415, −0.033, −0.110 against antecedent rainfall

Isolated where the signal is lost: raw bare-soil LST correlates at +0.414, but that is the seasonal cycle; deseasonalised it is +0.026, and NDVI over the same scenes and rainfall series responds at +0.453 as a positive control
Quantified a structural flaw of thermal trapezoids: the hot-edge intercept drifts 67.7 K across scenes while the trapezoid is only 6.1 K deep, an 11:1 drift-to-signal ratio
Only 198 of 302 scenes contain both a bare and a vegetated population, so per-scene fitting is under-constrained while pooling is invalid — the method is caught between two failure modes
Study area chosen by measuring the terrain confound within scenes: Swat and Chagai fail at measured lapse rates of −5.1 and −9.6 K/km, which pooled analysis hides entirely

gallery.caption: TOTRAM before and after, 2022 — and it reads backwards: June wet, September dry, because W is normalised per month
Where the signal is lost: deseasonalised LST carries none, while NDVI (control) responds
Five trapezoid specifications against the OPTRAM benchmark
The thermal trapezoid drifts 67.7 K across scenes but is only 6.1 K deep
Thermal vs optical retrieval, 73 matched dates: uncorrelated

title: Drought Monitoring with SPI — Tharparkar District, Pakistan
description: Standardized Precipitation Index over Pakistan's recurrent-famine district, built on 44 years of CHIRPS rainfall (1981–2024). SPI fits a gamma distribution, which has zero density at zero — but 53.7% of pixel-months in Tharparkar have exactly zero rainfall. The study quantifies what that breaks, and where the index should refuse to answer at all.
highlights: Applied the textbook way, SPI produces a 95% false-alarm rate on its most severe category: 118 months flagged as extreme drought, 112 of them near-normal once zero-inflation is handled
Naive vs corrected differ by RMS 1.252 SPI units — wider than an entire McKee drought category
SPI-1 is undefined in 8 of 12 months here; the gamma fit is refused below 20 non-zero years rather than returning a number for a rainless month
Spatial averaging hides the whole problem: the district-mean series reports SPI-1 as fittable in all 12 months, the pixels report 8 of 12 as unfittable
CHIRPS DAILY gives 53.7% zero months over the same pixels where CHIRPS PENTAD gives 0.0% — the product choice decides whether the problem is even visible
Independent validation: ranking 44 years recovers 1987 and 2002 as driest (the documented 1999–2002 Sindh drought) and 2011 and 2022 as wettest, both flood years

gallery.caption: SPI-12 before and after: drought year 1987 vs flood year 2011, Tharparkar District
Cost of skipping zero-inflation: naive SPI pins ordinary dry months at extreme drought
Where SPI may legitimately be computed — SPI-1 fails in 8 of 12 months
SPI-12 and SPI-3, 1981–2024, zero-inflated gamma
Study-area screening: monsoon vs winter-westerly regimes have complementary usable months

title: Post-Flood NDVI Change Detection — Layyah District, 2022
description: Sentinel-2 NDVI change detection after the 2022 Pakistan floods, built on a control-year design that separates flood damage from the ordinary double-cropping cycle, and cross-checked against an independently derived Sentinel-1 radar flood extent.
highlights: 1,232 km² (19.4%) of material vegetation loss concentrated along the Indus belt, against 2,084 km² of gain where the same rainfall greened the semi-arid Thal
Raw June→October NDVI change was +0.071, but control years give +0.076 — almost the entire raw signal is crop phenology, not flood damage
Independent radar cross-check: mean NDVI anomaly −0.088 inside the SAR flood extent vs −0.021 outside, a 0.067 separation between two physically unrelated sensors
District mean anomaly of −0.005 would imply no impact; the result only survives as a map, and the write-up says so rather than quoting the reassuring number

title: SAR Flood Detection — Layyah District, 2022 Pakistan Floods
description: Scene-by-scene Sentinel-1 change detection across the 2022 monsoon, mapping the full inundation curve rather than a single composite. Separates riverine overflow from pluvial ponding, which the two spatial populations in the data support.
highlights: Peak inundation 95.4 km² (1.50% of district) on 2022-07-20; two flood waves resolved
Compositing a multi-week 'after' window understated peak extent 3× (40 km² vs 95 km²)
Mixed relative orbits inflated detected area ~2× with no ground change; orbit 5 covers 99.9% of the district, orbit 107 only 20.9%
Dual-polarisation water test (VV ≤ −18 dB AND VH ≤ −25 dB) removes false detection over radar-dark Thal desert sand

title: Optical Soil Moisture with OPTRAM — Layyah District, Pakistan
description: Sentinel-2 surface soil moisture over Layyah District using the OPTRAM trapezoid model, with the trapezoid edges fitted by quantile regression instead of drawn by eye, and the retrieval validated against antecedent rainfall and ERA5-Land. The straightforward version of the method returns a soil-moisture product that anti-correlates with rainfall; the study is built around finding out why.
highlights: Bare-soil relative saturation nearly doubled after the 2022 flood, 0.219 → 0.413 (+89%)
The district-mean retrieval anti-correlates with rainfall (r = −0.372) because OPTRAM reads canopy water where the canopy is closed; masked to bare soil it tracks antecedent rainfall at r = +0.855
Cloud masking biases the wet windows: valid-pixel fraction correlates with reference soil moisture at r = −0.756, so the wettest periods are sampled from their driest, clearest fraction
Trapezoid edges fitted over 23,991 observations (2019–2024): dry edge R² = 0.947, wet edge R² = 0.990
Study area chosen by measurement, not convenience — 6 candidate districts scored on trapezoid quality; 3 fail outright, including an urban negative control

gallery.caption: OPTRAM surface soil moisture before and after the 2022 flood, Layyah District
Validation: bare soil tracks antecedent rainfall (r = +0.86), the district mean inverts it
Fitted NDVI–STR trapezoid, 23,991 observations, 2019–2024
Study-area selection: trapezoid quality across six candidate districts

title: Surface Soil Moisture from SAR — Layyah District
description: Relative surface soil moisture via TU Wien change detection, referenced to per-pixel dry/wet extremes from an 8-year Sentinel-1 stack and validated against ERA5-Land reanalysis and CHIRPS rainfall.
highlights: District mean rose 39.7% → 76.0% between June and August 2022; 91.3% of the district retained after masking
Validated over 36 months: r = 0.489 vs ERA5-Land, r = 0.477 vs CHIRPS rainfall
Dry-season divergence from reanalysis is consistent with canal irrigation that ERA5-Land does not model — reported as an open question, not a resolved finding
References taken as P5/P95 of monthly medians, since min/max are single-observation statistics driven by speckle

title: Multi-Temporal SAR Crop Mapping — Layyah District
description: Crop mapping from 24 monthly Sentinel-1 composites across a full rabi–kharif crop year, resolving five cropping systems over 3,995 km² of cropland. Split into a validated stage and an inferred one, since no crop-type ground truth exists for Pakistan in the Earth Engine catalogue.
highlights: Supervised cropland mask: overall accuracy 0.825, κ = 0.651 on a disjoint held-out split; 3,995 km² cropland
Five cropping systems mapped: wheat–cotton double crop (1,359 km²), cotton (940 km²), sugarcane/orchard (810 km²), fallow (579 km²), wheat/gram (308 km²)
Crop labels derived from each class's seasonal phenology by rank, not hardcoded to cluster IDs, so they survive a change of seed or period
Separability analysis reports confidence honestly: wheat/gram is distinct at 3.5–6.9 dB, while cotton, double-crop and perennial sit within ~1 dB
Identified a district-wide March backscatter spike as a shared rainfall event (55.5 mm), not crop phenology

title: Multi-Temporal Speckle Filtering — Layyah District
description: Quegan–Yu multi-temporal speckle filtering over a 62-scene single-orbit Sentinel-1 stack, benchmarked against a spatial filter tuned to identical smoothness so the comparison actually isolates the multi-temporal advantage.
highlights: Equivalent Number of Looks improved ×3.47 (3.31 → 11.50) across the district
At matched ENL the filter strictly dominates a boxcar: smoother (11.50 vs 9.50) and 1.46× the edge retention
Filter implemented in linear power space — averaging in dB biases results low and understates the gain
ENL measured over a homogeneous desert patch as well as district-wide, since cropland variance is real signal
